name: Baunscheidtism

lead: Baunscheidtism is a historical treatment developed by German mechanic Carl Baunscheidt (1809-1873). A spring device called the Lebenswecker, or artificial leech, pricked the skin with many fine needles and an irritant oil was applied so that the skin became inflamed.

Practitioners believed the resulting inflammation drew the body's attention away from illness. Among conditions it was promoted for were whooping cough, toothache, mental disorders and baldness, which is its link to hair and appearance.

paras: The device was pressed to the skin to make a pattern of small punctures, and a toxic oil was rubbed in to provoke a rash. Its popularity led to counterfeit devices in the 19th century.
The method deliberately irritates and breaks the skin, so infection, scarring and pigment changes are plausible. Its legitimacy was questioned by at least 1880.

angle.text: Baunscheidt's followers claimed his treatment could remedy baldness by inflaming the scalp. No clinical trial of the method is recorded.

lead: Baunscheidtism is a 19th-century treatment system named after Carl Baunscheidt (1809-1873), a German mechanic and inventor.[1][2] Its device, the Lebenswecker or artificial leech, used many fine needles to puncture the skin before an irritant oil was applied.[2]

Followers believed the induced inflammation drew the body's attention away from illness, and claims included cures for whooping cough, toothaches, mental disorders and baldness.[2] The appearance link is therefore through scalp stimulation for hair loss.
A pharmaceutical history article documents Baunscheidt's life and the therapy.[1] Wikipedia classes it as a form of pseudoscience, and its legitimacy was questioned in 19th-century Australia.[2]

paras: The Lebenswecker was a spring-loaded needle device that punctured the skin, followed by application of a toxic oil to cause inflammation.[2] The underlying idea resembled other counter-irritation therapies: inflammation in the skin was believed to divert the body's attention and aid recovery from disease.[2]

Carl Baunscheidt was a German mechanic and inventor whose device became popular enough to be counterfeited.[2] A museum record dates one instrument to 1865-1875.[2] In 1880 a Melbourne practitioner who was a bootmaker rather than a doctor lost a lawsuit for payment, one of the early public challenges to the therapy's legitimacy.[2] A 1989 article in Pharmaceutical Historian covers his biography.[1]
